name: Blood Orange
lede: Blood Orange is a deep, red-leaning orange named for the fruit with crimson flesh.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
The name is a fruit description, and the library records it in several systems: the RAL paint code 2002, and Maerz and Paul's dictionary, which dates the name to 1890 [1]. It sits between [[orange]] and [[red]], and its nearest neighbors in our data are reds [1].

Finlay uses the fruit as a comparison: medieval artists infused saffron in egg-white glair as a cheap alternative to gold leaf, and when she tried it herself, it had become the color of blood oranges overnight [3]. On paper, she adds, the paint was luminous, though not really like gold [3]. The books we hold say little else about the color [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Blood Orange appears in 0.89% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, as photographed [2]. It peaks in the 1400s at 4.0% of that century's paintings, 3.2 times the museums' baseline [2]. Inside a painting it is almost always an accent, in 96% of cases [2]. The painter who uses it most is Caravaggio, in 4 of 47 works here, though no painter stands out against the baseline [2]. It is most over-represented in Indian paintings, at 3.2 times expected [2].

openers: Blood Orange is almost always an accent in the paintings that hold it, as photographed.

issues: Finlay's saffron-glair passage was her own experiment, and the paint was luminous but not gold-like; reworded.
